definition: Inactive or resting for a time but still able to become active again later.
example: The seeds stayed dormant in the dry soil until the spring rains finally arrived.
nuance: Dormant means activity is paused and could start again, unlike extinct, which means it has ended for good.
prompt: A geologist describes a volcano that has not erupted in several centuries.
options: The volcano is dormant, so scientists still watch it for signs of waking.
The dormant volcano has been pouring out lava every day this week.
The dormant volcano towers over the other peaks and controls the region's weather.
Because it is dormant, the volcano can never erupt again under any conditions.
reasons: A quiet volcano that could erupt again is exactly the kind that stays under watch.
Daily eruptions mean the volcano is active, the reverse of resting.
This confuses the word with dominant, which describes power or prominence.
A volcano that can never erupt is extinct; a resting one may still wake up.

practice.prompt: A retired man finds his old violin in the attic after thirty years.
options: As the dormant member of the family band, he chose every song they played.
His dormant love of music was gone forever, so he gave the violin away.
After a few weeks of practice, his dormant skill came back to life.
His dormant practice routine had him playing six hours every single day.
reasons: Being in charge describes a dominant member, a look-alike with a different meaning.
Something gone forever is dead or extinct; the word implies it could return.
An ability that sat unused for decades and then returned fits the word well.
A demanding daily schedule is constant activity, not a pause.
